rationale: Evidence: the best raced score is 39.81 (iterations 3, 5 and 6). Iterations 5 and 6 are the same design, and iteration 5 is the best-tested one: wheel_track 0.12, wheel_radius 0.03, kp 3.0, ki 0.8, kd 0.03, base_speed 1.5, five sensors at x -0.032 to +0.032, y 0.05, size 0.012, weights -1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1, last_direction. Every run in the record ended off track at about 0.06 m, not at the 3 s limit, so the early departure is the binding failure. The Round-2 critique is right that the revision was not a clean test. The revision compared against the wrong baseline: it kept wheel_track 0.14 and the kp 1.5 / ki 1.0 / kd 0.1 / base 1.0 controller from iteration 7, which scored 26 and 36.7, not 39.8. So it differed from the best run in several variables at once, and its claim to differ in only wheel_radius was false. I reject that design. I keep the iteration-5 design exactly and change only wheel_radius from 0.03 to 0.04. Accepted from the critique: the wheel_radius change also raises steering authority about 1.33x (speed and yaw rate per unit turn both scale with radius), so a result cannot be attributed to speed alone; line loss (2 events per run on oval, slalom and s-bend) is a real score cost, so I note it for the next iteration. Rejected: the base_speed 0.6 suggestion, since runs end by departure rather than the time limit, and cutting ground speed would not help. Expected result: higher ground speed per PWM, so progress rises above the 0.1675 oval, 0.0725 s-bend and 0.0625 slalom baselines, with max_error near 0.061 to 0.066. Success means a score above 39.81. If steering_oscillation exceeds 0.25 or max_error grows, the larger effective gain is the cause, and the next step is wheel_radius 0.035 or a lower kp.
